meaning_mnemonic: The radical for foot and the kanji for foot are exactly the same. That being said, there's also another meaning you should keep in mind, which is sufficient. If you think about it, one foot should be sufficient enough to walk around with if you hop.
reading_mnemonic: What do you wear on your foot? You wear a sock (そく).

meaning_mnemonic: If your car runs into a cloud you'll revolve around it instead of going straight through. Clouds are really hard to see through, so even though you're trying not to, you revolve in a tight circle up and around the cloud anyway.
reading_mnemonic: You have to revolve around the cloud ten (てん) times before it disappears and you're able to go through.

meaning_mnemonic: Someone on a scooter has an axe, and they're getting near to you really fast! Oh no, they're so close now, you need to get out of here!
reading_mnemonic: As they draw near, you recognize who is riding the scooter: the King (きん) of England! Behind him, a bunch of his guards also on scooters and wielding axes appear and move close to you.

meaning_mnemonic: On its scooter, a creature with horns from heaven will take things you want to send there.
reading_mnemonic: You want to send your soul (そう) to heaven. I mean, you don't want it to go to some of those other places you've heard of, so why not send your soul?

meaning_mnemonic: There's a scooter with your mama carrying a task she needs to get done. You see her pass through, hurrying by to get that task done.
reading_mnemonic: As you watch your mama pass through the house, she yells, "YOU HAVE TO DO THIS TASK TOO (つう)!" Too?! Oh no, now you have to do it too. Hurry up!

meaning_mnemonic: Use a scooter to travel the circumference of the world and it will take you a full week. Seven whole days!
reading_mnemonic: If you want to scoot for a week, you'll need shoes (しゅう). Good shoes too, not sandals or high heels or boots. Solid, high quality shoes, so you don't fall off the scooter and hurt yourself.

meaning_mnemonic: While riding your scooter, you bang your forehead on the car in front. Your scooter's wrecked, so you have to carry it home. You'll need a lot of luck to get that scooter home safely.
reading_mnemonic: As you carry the scooter, your luck turns, and it starts to rain, so you pull out your umbrella (うん). Now you're holding your scooter, your forehead, and an umbrella.

meaning_mnemonic: Aim the scooter's neck at the road! Scooters are only meant for driving on streets and paths, and if you go the wrong way, you'll probably break your own neck!
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading どう we use the word "doughnut." You're traveling down this road so fast that you don't see the giant doughnut (どう) that's rolling toward you until the last minute. You crash into it, and both you and the doughnut go tumbling down. Ahg, your neck!

meaning_mnemonic: The heavy radical and the heavy kanji are the same.
reading_mnemonic: In your hand is a very heavy jewel (じゅう). Real jewels are always heavier than they look.

meaning_mnemonic: The village beforehand (what the village was before it was a village) was a field.
reading_mnemonic: On this field, the Yankees (や) used to play.

meaning_mnemonic: Gold, at its root, is made up of silver. Using silver as the root of a coin is a great way to save on gold! That's why, often, if you just scratch gold, you'll find there's silver hidden underneath, at its root.
reading_mnemonic: If you want to hunt for some silver for yourself, all you need is a guinea (ぎん) pig. Guinea pigs can smell silver, so get a couple and set them loose in the woods and they'll lead you straight to it.

meaning_mnemonic: A gate with a lantern is open for you. That's convenient, since it's pretty dark out and you might not have seen the open gate without the lantern's help.
reading_mnemonic: This open gate is in the water though, so you'll need a kayak (かい) to get in. Luckily, you've been carrying your kayak with you just in case.

meaning_mnemonic: This building has a roof and will teach you about the origin of many things. It's an institution!
reading_mnemonic: What does institution start with? In (いん)!

meaning_mnemonic: You chase a turkey up a tree to collect it. At least, you will once you've gathered enough turkeys into this one tree.
reading_mnemonic: Once you've collected enough turkeys, you're going to turn them into a shoe (しゅう). Maybe even two shoes, but that will mean gathering even more turkeys!

meaning_mnemonic: The blue radical and the blue kanji are exactly the same. Additionally, this can also mean young. You can remember this because young people have potential as limitless as the blue sky!
reading_mnemonic: You've been feeling really blue. Mostly because your skin, hair, and eyes have all turned blue. It was an out-of-the-blue transformation! But now someone places his hand on your shoulder and points at your saber (せい). It's blue too! You aren't alone!

meaning_mnemonic: For some reason, you are standing on the sun. It's obviously very hot, but the thing you notice most is the sound of you burning up.
reading_mnemonic: This sound isn't just loud, it's familiar. Finally you place it: onions (おん)!

meaning_mnemonic: The sun shines down on your coat rack to reveal your geoduck-patterned jacket, which then becomes the major topic of discussion all around town.
reading_mnemonic: After a few days, the topic changes from the cool geoduck design to what kind of dye (だい) you used to get those real-to-life geoduck colors.

meaning_mnemonic: You look at a table and notice it is being used as a slide by insects to launch themselves into the wind. This kanji can also mean style. To remember this, consider how styles can change quickly, just like the wind!
reading_mnemonic: You wonder what's pushing these insects to jump into the wind in such a manner, and you realize that it's because they've had way too much food (ふう).

meaning_mnemonic: You might want to eat, but your anti-eating stance means your meal will just sit in front of you, uneaten. Food is meant to be eaten! Stop trying to fast and take a bite.
reading_mnemonic: As you stare at the meal, Han (はん) Solo appears before you and takes a bite! This is what happens if you don't eat your food, someone else will eat it.

meaning_mnemonic: You can eat all you want, but you'll still lack something to drink. You can't live just from eating, you have to drink things too!
reading_mnemonic: You get desperate for a drink and put some nori (の) seaweed in a blender, trying to create a drink of your own.

meaning_mnemonic: Eating the roof is a bear, because the roof is a public building. Because it is a public building bears are allowed to eat the roof.
reading_mnemonic: Public buildings must make their roofs available for eating because of a law passed by Genghis Khan (かん).

meaning_mnemonic: A horse and a shrimp are sitting next to each other. They are both at the train station, waiting for a train to come and take them home.
reading_mnemonic: The train pulls into the station. They walk up to the train doors, but they don't open. "Perhaps a key (えき) would help?" asks the station master, as he goes over to open the door to the train.

meaning_mnemonic: A horse and a squid are going to test you.
reading_mnemonic: The test is being supervised by Ken (けん) the samurai.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical fish and the kanji fish are exactly the same!
reading_mnemonic: You catch a fish. As you pull it out of the water, it starts yelling and pointing: "GO!" (ぎょ). "GO GYO GYO GYO!" There's a huge cruise ship coming right towards your little fishing boat. No wonder the fish was yelling GO at you.

meaning_mnemonic: The bird radical and the bird kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: Think of a run-of-the-mill bird, whatever comes to mind for you first is fine. Then, your lovely bird swells. The shape of a face, then a hand, start stretching the bird apart until it explodes outward. Covered in blood and feathers is Mrs. Chou (ちょう).

meaning_mnemonic: The radical black and the kanji black are exactly the same.
reading_mnemonic: You're in a completely black room. There's no way out, and you can't see. The room starts to fill with liquid. It gets in your mouth. You taste it. It's Coke (こく)! Mm, tasty Coke.

meaning_mnemonic: As you dig under the ground you discover a head resting near a mountain, which are both strange things to find beneath the earth.
reading_mnemonic: But, you dig too deep and water flows into where you are. Your only hope is a row (りょう) boat floating off in the distance.

meaning_mnemonic: You put a grain in your mouth and let it take a ride. This kanji has the same radicals as 和, but this time the grain is in your mouth, which is why there's little pieces of grain sticking out of the 口 part ;)
reading_mnemonic: You decide the grain is probably lonely on this ride alone, so you add some nori (の) seaweed, so it has a friend.

meaning_mnemonic: What does your mama tell you to do in the street? Look before you cross! You gotta do it beforehand, or it could be too late.
reading_mnemonic: As you look beforehand, you see a yo-yo (よ) lying in the street.

meaning_mnemonic: In prison, Wolverine gets picked on for the barbs coming out of his hands. This creates a lot of conflict between him and the other prisoners. They don't take kindly to mutants, and Wolverine doesn't take kindly to bigots — hence the conflict.
reading_mnemonic: This constant conflict between Wolverine and the other inmates is really affecting his soul (そう). Despite what people think, Wolverine really doesn't like to fight. He just hates injustice so much, he feels he has to do something about it.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical death and the kanji death are the same.
reading_mnemonic: Your death will be because of a bowling (ぼう) accident. Oh, you didn't know? You're going to be hit by a giant bowling ball and crushed flat.

meaning_mnemonic: You put a lid on your father. But, he won't taste good alone, so you mix in some other ingredients. They mingle inside the pot with him.
reading_mnemonic: With a mix of your father and other ingredients mingling in your cooking pot, you lift up the lid... your father pops up. Your father is こういち. He stares back at you with a big smile.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader of alligators... she's no ordinary leader, that's for sure. She's not a politician, she's not a queen... She's one of the Other Ones, a group of strange, eccentric people who become leaders of animals.
reading_mnemonic:
To remember the reading た, we use the word "taco":

Then there's the others of the others. These are the taco (た) worshipers. They're really strange.

meaning_mnemonic: When you take your leader's measurements, you realize they're too short, so you attach things to them to make the measurements more impressive. Attach some heels to the shoes, then attach another head on top of theirs. There — perfect measurements thanks to these attachments.
reading_mnemonic: You have to remember the kun'yomi reading of this kanji, and the part you need to remember is つ. So, think of how you would attach something to something else. What would you need? You'd need two (つ) things to put together!

meaning_mnemonic: The leader of the cow tribe is too important to deal with small matters and trivial affairs.
reading_mnemonic: All of his affairs are taken care of by Ken (けん) the samurai, who he hired as his underling.

meaning_mnemonic: Both a leader and a king have a duty to protect their people. A good leader always protects his followers, and a good king always protects his subjects. This is their duty.
reading_mnemonic: You’re the village nincompoop (にん), but the king and the leader still have a duty to protect you. Even a nincompoop is important to the kings and leaders of the world.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader has a cloud that he uses to transmit all of the messages he needs to send to his people. The cloud floats above him and when he wants to tell people something he just whispers into the cloud and it transmits his message really, really loudly to all of them.
reading_mnemonic: As the leader transmits his latest series of messages to you and the others, you notice a pretty large dent (でん) in it. That dent is probably a clue to what this cloud is really made of.

meaning_mnemonic: A leader stands at the highest rank in an organization. The leader is of the highest rank and stands above all others.
reading_mnemonic: This great leader is actually the leader of the boy scouts. And as we all know, the highest rank in boy scouts is the rank of eagle (い) scout. This great leader has attained the rank of eagle scout and stands above all other scouts.

meaning_mnemonic: Regardless of whether or not you wear a hat while you jackhammer, you’re going to have a surplus of noise. Jackhammers are loud, and your hat is doing nothing to dampen the racket. There’s a surplus of commotion coming from the jackhammer and onlookers are not amused.
reading_mnemonic: One of the people walking by is the owner of a push cart yo-yo (よ) stand. Having a surplus of yo-yos, he starts throwing them at you. This makes you stop using the jackhammer as you need both hands to fend off the yo-yo barrage.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader of the yakuza shows you his knife. He says, "This is an example of a knife."
reading_mnemonic: "This is an example," the leader of the yakuza tells you. "Next time, I'll show you an example of a ray (れい) gun."

meaning_mnemonic: A leader stands upon the ground of the rice paddy. She is searching for treasure. It is said that this treasure here in this rice field will make things much easier for the leader (that's what leaders really want, after all). If she gets this treasure, it will be a great convenience for her, because convenience is everything when you're the leader.
reading_mnemonic: She finds a place to dig in the ground. It looks like there's some fresh dirt here. Finally, the treasure of convenience that will make this leader's life so much easier. She digs into the ground and pulls out a box. When she opens it, she finds out it's a bento (べん). "My god," she thinks. "This really will make my life more convenient. My people can take their lunches with them now instead of coming back to base to eat, which will waste way less time!"
radical_breakdown: ｲ|Leader, 一|Ground, 田|Rice Paddy, メ|Treasure

meaning_mnemonic: A psychic leader kneels to the ground, picks up a thread, and instantly makes a connection with the person that it came from. This leader is very powerful, so even a thread is enough for them to make a psychic connection with the person who was wearing it.
reading_mnemonic: As you develop this psychic connection with the owner of the thread, you can tell that they're currently eating a cake (けい).

meaning_mnemonic: To your leader, you say: "Believe and trust in me." The leader doesn't think you can handle your duties, so you have to say this to him. You want him to believe and trust that you're responsible. You can handle this task.
reading_mnemonic: As you face your leader and say "Believe and trust in me," you kneel down on each shin (しん). You have shin splints, so it hurts a bit, but you do it anyway to show how serious you are.

meaning_mnemonic: Someone stabbed the leader mole with a knife to overthrow it. Now there is a new mole leader. Because that's what happens when you overthrow someone—someone else needs to take over. In this case, a vengeful mole.
reading_mnemonic: Where do leaders get overthrown the most? In とうきょう. Just think back in Japanese history, back when everyone was at war with one another. People were taking over and getting overthrown and then that guy gets overthrown and then THAT guy gets overthrown. Basically, it used to be hard to stay a leader in とうきょう.

meaning_mnemonic: The leader of the shellfish has a knife in its side. It's fine though, don't worry, it's just a reminder that he won the great shellfish war back when they were trying to choose the new leader.
reading_mnemonic: Because of this knife in his side, he can't pronounce certain words correctly. The most obvious one is when he says 川 (かわ), but it comes out of the side of his mouth as がわ.

meaning_mnemonic: Your leader makes you lift heavy loads with all your power, since this is what you do for work. Why do you do this kind of work? Well, you're good at it and the leader makes you do it, I guess.
reading_mnemonic: Where do you get the power to do all this work? From doughnuts (どう). You eat nothing but doughnuts. If you had no doughnuts, you couldn't work. In fact, your leader pays you for your work… in doughnuts.

meaning_mnemonic: You see a triceratops in the distance. But, it's odd. It's perfectly pi shaped (that is, circular, like a pie). Some kind of piceratops, if you will. The reason they are this shape is because they want to absorb as much light as possible. They evolved to be round so they don't have any corners casting a shadow.
reading_mnemonic: As you watch this majestic beast absorbing light, suddenly several dozen feral こういちs burst out from the wilderness, spears in hand. Oh no! Those こういちs are hunting this rare piceratops!

meaning_mnemonic: The hat crowns the king, because all kings must have one.
reading_mnemonic: But, as you're going through all the kings, it turns out not all of them have hats after all. The last one you come to is hatless. He's the king of Zen (ぜん). He has simple clothes and a shaved head, unlike all the other fancy kings standing around nearby.

meaning_mnemonic: The card game fish are best at is blackjack because they can easily hold the cards with their fins together. In blackjack you don't have to have a huge hand, full of cards. It's just a few, so fish fins can keep them together and just hit or stay.
reading_mnemonic: Once a year trillions of fish get together in きょうと to play blackjack. They have a huge tournament there once a year.

meaning_mnemonic: There's an eye on the ground, among some fins. What happened? You killed a fish, and now you must hide the murder tool. Quick, hide the tool before someone finds out it was you.
reading_mnemonic: The tool is dripping with goo (ぐ). Goopy, incriminating goo. It's the guts of the fish you just killed and it's all over your hands too. Yuck.

meaning_mnemonic: Your head has a person inside it!
reading_mnemonic: You know this kanji means inside, so you can keep thinking about the person that's inside you, running around. You finally discover him, and try to take him out, but before you can, he pulls out a knife (ない) and threatens to cut you if you do anything irrational.

meaning_mnemonic: Take your yakuza knife and put it in a row with the others.
reading_mnemonic: Should we put them in a row? Let's (れつ) put them in a row!

meaning_mnemonic: You wear a special outfit and equip a sword whenever you do something for the first time. Doing something for the first time is always scary, but the right outfit and a sword at your side can give you the confidence and courage to overcome your jitters!
reading_mnemonic: So, what is it you're doing for the first time? A fashion show (しょ). Your special outfit and sword aren't just to calm your nerves — they're also what you'll be showing off on the catwalk.

meaning_mnemonic: I hereby cut your assets in half with a knife, says the judge. At someone's divorce proceedings. Ah, the oldest judge trick in the book.
reading_mnemonic: This judge is Han (はん) Solo, so you know he's not going to back down.

meaning_mnemonic: Cut grains with a knife to make them smaller and you'll make a great profit. By cutting them, now you can get three grains worth of money for what was once a single grain.
reading_mnemonic: To make an even better profit, you decide to cut up reeds (り) too. You stuff the grains in the reeds and sell that as "self-cooking" sets.

meaning_mnemonic: Cows, using nothing more than a towel and a knife, have taken control of the world. Their system of control is brutal — payback for how we humans have treated them, I guess.
reading_mnemonic: It's time to take control back from the cows! Pull out your saber (せい) and fight back!

meaning_mnemonic: The power of your mouth lets you add words together to form a sentence. Marvel at the mighty additive power your mouth holds! You add words together in an amazing fashion!
reading_mnemonic: Your parents are so proud of you being able to add words together that they surprise you with a new car (か). Wow! You add some stickers to your bumper and add your favorite playlist to the car radio. Let's drive.

meaning_mnemonic: With top hat power, you're able to help anyone.
reading_mnemonic: The person you help with your top hat power? It's Jo-Anne (じょ).

meaning_mnemonic: A woman sits on a stool to conserve her power, as her servants toil away in the kitchen. They toil away preparing a feast for this powerful woman while she kicks back on her cozy stool. She's a queen and deserves to be pampered.
reading_mnemonic: As a servant you toil not just for the woman, but also for her dog (ど). Anything she gets, the dog gets too. That means double the toil for you. But hey, at least the dog is cute.

meaning_mnemonic: A Viking in a position of power does not need to labor in the fields. Labor is for the weak! A Viking of power takes what he wants, and need not labor for it. A powerful Viking plunders all and takes what he wants!
reading_mnemonic: It takes a lot of labor to harvest roe (ろう) so that’s what the Viking decides to take first! Roe is delicious, but it’s small and delicate. Vikings don’t labor for their own roe! They take it and eat it!

meaning_mnemonic: You use a special spear in winter to give yourself the power to do all of your tasks.
reading_mnemonic: Your task is to spear this cow. "Moo (む)!" it yells at you and runs away. You need to make dinner though... that's your task, so you better catch up to that cow and put an end to its mooing.

meaning_mnemonic: The moon grants a gladiator its power so he will win! Victory will be his!
reading_mnemonic: He wins over and over again, and soon the Shougun (しょう) is even rooting for him. In fact, the Shougun claims him as his personal gladiator of choice.

meaning_mnemonic: A leader with a spoon is a powerful thing. Even something as ordinary as a spoon can create great change in the world when given to the right person.
reading_mnemonic: Then, this hero of yours takes their spoon and says some magic words into it, changing it into a car (か).

meaning_mnemonic: The simple radical and the simple kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: One of the most simple things in the world is getting a tan (たん). All you have to do is stand outside long enough. It doesn't matter what skin type you have or what the weather is like. Eventually, if you stand out there long enough, you'll get a tan.

meaning_mnemonic: There is a prison on a cliff surrounded by snakes. Now that's a dangerous place. If you try to escape the prison you either fall to your death off the cliff or get bitten/squeezed to death by the snakes. Can you think of anything more dangerous than this? I can't.
reading_mnemonic: Lucky for you, even though you're stuck in this dangerous place, there is hope. There is a key (き). All dangerous prisons have a key. You just have to find and steal it so you can avoid the cliffs and snakes!

meaning_mnemonic: The original radical and the original kanji are the same! This kanji can also mean field, probably because that's what everything originally looked like before humans: just a bunch of fields.
reading_mnemonic: The original Japanese hero was Genji (げん), from "The Tale of Genji."

meaning_mnemonic: You try to be private, but because of your big hair you end up having to participate in everything. Can you imagine people asking for volunteers or something, and you trying to look inconspicuous with your big hair? Of course they're going to notice you and make you participate.
reading_mnemonic: You know who has big hair and loves to participate in everything? Santa-san (さん)! Well, his hair is more big on the bottom (it's a beard) than whatever you have on your head, but hair is hair. And he participates in present-giving in every house in the world! See? Big hair = participation!

meaning_mnemonic: Under a cliff there's a stool. If someone has a stool deep inside a cliff, they are most likely pretty anti-society, hiding away like that.
reading_mnemonic: Turns out, when you go to this guy and pull off his beard, its the anti-hero from Star Wars, Han (はん) Solo! What is Han doing here, so hidden away? He's obviously hiding from Jabba because he doesn't want to get frozen in carbonite again.

meaning_mnemonic: There's an ear just sitting on a stool. Nobody's watching, so, you take it.
reading_mnemonic: You're the kind of person who likes to take things. "What things?" you ask. Little toes (と). Because that isn't creepy.

meaning_mnemonic: Someone throws a cleat at your forehead while you sit on a stool. You must accept this. Then another guy cleats you in the forehead, but you remain on the stool and receive it without complaint. This is some kind of acceptance ritual for the most prestigious Spanish soccer club in the world. If a cleat to the forehead doesn't knock you off the stool, you'll receive an offer to join.
reading_mnemonic: After they accept you, they give you a small juice (じゅ) box. It's to help you recover from the trauma of getting kicked. And you receive the juice with grace.

meaning_mnemonic: There's a mouth in the ground (in our case, it's a hatch), and inside is some kind of prison you can't quite get to. If you've ever seen Lost, this will sound familiar... on the hatch, there's actually a series of numbers that you don't understand.
reading_mnemonic: "You want to know the number to the hatch?" yells an old voice from inside. You say "yes," and the voice gives you the numbers and you're in! You go down into the prison, where there is one prisoner: Grandpa ごういち. Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち.

meaning_mnemonic: The radical suit and the kanji suit are exactly the same! This kanji can also mean join which makes sense. When something suits you well, like a hat or something, it joins together with you quite well too. Join me, my hat! You suit my head well. It just fits, you know?
reading_mnemonic: You need someone who will suit you. Someone who can join you on your life journey. So you call Grandpa ごういち. Note: For the ごう reading mnemonics, we use Grandpa ごういち because こういち is used for the こう reading. So just remember that ごう comes from Koichi's grandpa ごういち.

meaning_mnemonic: A drop hits your mustache. Where did it come from? "Ah, it came from yonder," you say, facing that way.
reading_mnemonic: Who shot this drop at you from yonder? You look over yonder, and see a figure. It is こういち.

meaning_mnemonic: Wolverine is going down a slide and from your mouth you scream, "Hey, buddy! Watch it with that slide, it's really fast and you might hurt yourself, buddy!" You're a really good buddy to Wolverine. He also happens to be the local ruler of these lands. You make it a habit to befriend the local strongmen, just in case… No wonder you're so buddy-buddy with all the rulers around here.
reading_mnemonic: As you're about to embrace your buddy Wolverine, a coonhound (くん) tackles him off the slide, and bites him in the process.

meaning_mnemonic: You see a slide covered in dirt and use your mouth to clean it off. Then, you announce to everyone that the slide is clean and they can use it safely again.
reading_mnemonic: After you announce the slide is clean, you take a big swig of Coke (こく). The dirty slide left a nasty taste in your mouth, but the Coke is helping to wash it away.

meaning_mnemonic: Orders coming from your mouth will determine the fate of your soldiers. You are their commanding officer and your orders determine their life and death.
reading_mnemonic: You are the commanding officer on the Mayflower (めい). You give orders to colonize America. The orders spewing from your mouth hole determine the fate of the settlers and the fate of America and the fate of the world! You and the Mayflower have changed everything forever.

meaning_mnemonic: When everyone has grain in their mouth, you will have peace. That is the Japanese style of doing things.
reading_mnemonic: Peace is the Japanese style. The walruses (わ) living off of Japan see this, and start to emulate.

meaning_mnemonic: If there is a drum in your mouth it's time to rejoice! And because of your mouth drum your rejoicing will be loud and booming!
reading_mnemonic: You loudly rejoice for a while when suddenly someone runs over and shoves a key (き) in your mouth, locking it shut. You can't rejoice anymore! You need that key to unlock your mouth!

meaning_mnemonic: There's a mouth inside a mouth. But if you look even closer (not actually, but we're pretending), you can see another mouth inside that mouth... and another one inside of that one! It keeps going and going. Can you count the number of times there's a mouth inside a mouth? This kanji also means revolve too. Think of each "time" a thing happens, it loops back around and comes back to the beginning, revolving around again another time.
reading_mnemonic: If you're having a hard time wrapping your head around the infinite number of times these mouths revolve, just picture yourself in a little kayak (かい) going around and down through the mouths.

meaning_mnemonic: Your mouth is so big that it's the cause of all your problems.
reading_mnemonic: Your big mouth is the cause behind all your friends and family moving to an inn (いん). They move to the inn so they don't have to live with you and hear you talk anymore.

meaning_mnemonic: If you put your mouth on a tree and try to eat it, you’re probably a distressed and troubled individual (unless you’re a woodchuck). You don’t need to eat this tree, you have plenty of food at home. Get your mouth off that tree you distressed child.
reading_mnemonic: You thought you were the most distressed and troubled person in this situation, but then you look up and see a very equally distressed and troubled condor (こん). The tree you've been mouthing is its home. And now you've slobbered all over it, ruining this condor's day.

meaning_mnemonic: You examine the mouth of a zombie and find a small garden in there. There are even benches... it looks like a park.
reading_mnemonic: You look closer at the garden and suddenly everything ends (えん).

meaning_mnemonic: A narwhal sticks a stick into the dirt to see what might exist underneath it. Narwhals live in the sea, you see. So they're convinced nothing can exist anywhere else.
reading_mnemonic: The narwhal can't find anything but it can't stop thinking about what could exist outside of its world. It pulls out a xylophone (ざい) and starts tapping the keys with its horn. It plays a sad song about the meaning of life and whether existence is worth it.

meaning_mnemonic: You want to share happiness with people so you stamp stools with the news. Now when people want a report of all the happy things going on, they can just look down before they sit.
reading_mnemonic: You research and report the news from home (ほう). Only after, once all of the news is stamped onto the stools, do you leave your home.

meaning_mnemonic: The dirt mask is a mask which, when put on, will greatly increase the amount of dirt.
reading_mnemonic: Use the dirt mask to increase the dirt around you. The zombies (ぞう) are trying to escape, so you just keep increasing the dirt on top of them so they can't get out.

meaning_mnemonic: You have a samurai with a flag on a stick. On his flag is the symbol 声, the kanji for voice. Why does he have that there? He feels like his Shogun isn't giving him and his fellow Samurai a voice, so he's brought a flag with the word "voice" written on it to protest.
reading_mnemonic: You decide to join the samurai’s protest for more voice but immediately notice… they’re all 子, eh (こえ)?!

meaning_mnemonic: Again and again, winter changes you each year.
reading_mnemonic: You know what else changes each winter? Hens (へん)! They're constantly laying eggs, which then (possibly) turn into new hens.

meaning_mnemonic: A flowers net is upon your forehead in the evening. These appear on your head at night whenever you are having a dream.
reading_mnemonic: You dream about cows saying "moo (む), moo, moo!"
radical_breakdown: 艹|Flowers, 罒|Net, 冖|Forehead, 夕|Evening

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so this means fat.
reading_mnemonic: Imagine a fat person who loves to sleep on futon (ふと).

meaning_mnemonic: The husband radical and the husband kanji are the same. How useful, unlike some husbands, I'd imagine.
reading_mnemonic: What do all husbands love? Food (ふう)! Can you hear your future husband? He’s saying, "Fooooood! FOOOOOD!” like some kind of food craving zombie.

meaning_mnemonic: That slide is your husband's only fault. He loves that slide, more than you, and it's the only thing you don't like about him.
reading_mnemonic: You try to come up with another fault of his so you can complain, when you see a tiny shih tzu (しつ) trotting by. Oh no! Before you can call out, your husband has fallen off the slide and crushed the poor thing. You hear a sharp yelp and then nothing.

meaning_mnemonic: There is a woman and a child in front of you. You like them very much.
reading_mnemonic: "I like you two," you say to the woman and child. They both turn their heads 180 degrees back towards you. They both have faces that look just like こういち's. "We like you too," they say in unison.

meaning_mnemonic: You place a cross on a Wolverine woman. She's gone now, but she was once your wife.
reading_mnemonic: Wait a minute… She can't be dead because your wife is a cyborg (さい)! How could you forget?!

meaning_mnemonic: If a narwhal sticks a child with its horn then you have to admit that it exists. We know some of you have been doubting narwhals and whether they're real. Well now your kid is a kabob, so do you believe they exist now? I suppose you do.
reading_mnemonic: Oh, and the child we had to narwhal stab to prove they exist - that's your son (そん). Maybe you should have listened and kept your son out of the Narwhal Danger Zone (ぞん) after we warned you about it.

meaning_mnemonic: Your roof needs measurements done every year to make sure it will protect you properly.
reading_mnemonic: If the measurements are off, and your roof doesn't protect you, then you get to sue (す)! If you're still alive, that is.

meaning_mnemonic: The roof that became the origin of all roofs was perfect. It was tall and wide so it could fit and protect everyone. And the dimensions were perfect too.
reading_mnemonic: This perfect roof was commissioned by Genghis Khan (かん). We got all of the carpenters and home makers and construction workers he'd conquered together and tasked them with making the first roof, but only if they made it absolutely perfect.

meaning_mnemonic: Under this roof is a bear who works for the government. If you saw a bear out in the wild you might be afraid and try to run, but if you see a bear inside a building under a roof, don't be scared! It's just a government bear.
reading_mnemonic: The first government that allowed bears was set up by Genghis Khan (かん). He was all about conquering people and then using them as efficiently as possible. He discovered that bears are incredibly useful in government buildings as government workers.

meaning_mnemonic: You build a roof over your coat rack because you determine that this is the best way to protect your coats from the elements.
reading_mnemonic: Why did you determine your coat rack needed a roof? Because your coat pockets are full of tater (てい) tots! You can't afford to let your tater tots get rained on, so you determined they needed to be properly sheltered with a roof.

meaning_mnemonic: Climb onto the roof in spring to see the truth. The world is waking back up from winter and revealing the reality of what it is all around you.
reading_mnemonic: At the moment, you're trying to learn the truth about the deer that is coming out of the snowy woods when you see not one, but two baby deer appear with it! Gee! Two (じつ) babies! You keep looking around and realize that all of the animals seem to have two babies that they had hidden in the snow.

meaning_mnemonic: Under your roof in winter there are more mouths to feed because you let guests stay with you when it's cold. Some of them aren't family, so they have to pay to stay under your roof and get food. Those are customers.
reading_mnemonic: One of your guests is a regular named Kyaku (きゃく) the customer. Kyaku is always staying over at one place or another, so everyone knows their name.

meaning_mnemonic: You slip off the roof, your life flashes before your eyes, and you smash your mouth on the ground causing some serious damage. Oof, this is a really bad injury, you fell all the way off the roof and onto your mouth.
reading_mnemonic: As you try to assess the damage, you hear someone shout, "Guy (がい), hey, you okay, guy?" They run up to you, but your mouth is too damaged, you can't respond. "Okay guy, I'm gonna call you Guy now. Let's get you to the hospital."

meaning_mnemonic: If you put a roof over a valley it will change its form. Its appearance will alter completely!
reading_mnemonic: Its new appearance looks familiar to you, like it's a big yogurt (よう) cup! A valley with a roof on it looks exactly like a yogurt cup. Huh!

meaning_mnemonic: The roof under which the leader can house one hundred of his people is at the local lodge.
reading_mnemonic: The lodge shook (しゅく) as the hundred people came tumbling in through the door. It shook, but it didn't fall over. The roof stayed firmly in place, and everyone got to sleep under it okay.

meaning_mnemonic: The roof, even though it's almost spring, is still covered in ice so it's cold. Inside the house is cold, outside the house is cold. Everything is cold!
reading_mnemonic: You can't stand the cold anymore, so you hire a samurai (さむ) to come try to hack the ice off of your roof with his sword. You stand outside shivering, and watching as the samurai tries to stab the ice off of your roof.

meaning_mnemonic: From the roof, an icicle falls and hits Wolverine in the forehead, and he has to go over to the stool to lie down. And eventually he goes to sleep.
reading_mnemonic: While wolverine sleeps, he makes a horrible neighing (ね) sound. It's like there's a giant horse in his mouth screaming to get out! NEIGH NEIGH!
radical_breakdown: 宀|Roof, 丬|Icicle, ヨ|Wolverine, 冖|Forehead, 又|Stool

meaning_mnemonic: If you're on the roof of the festival you'll have to guess what's actually going on below you. You can kind of see that there are rides and maybe food? It smells like food. But you have to guess on the specifics because you're above it and not in it.
reading_mnemonic: To get a better guess, you ask Satsuki (さつ) for help. She's that little girl you know from some earlier mnemonics, and she happens to be up on the roof with you. Picture her as you ask, "What's your guess, Satsuki?"

meaning_mnemonic: Writing and measurement stand versus one another. Writing is all about feeling and expression. Measurement is about cold hard numbers. Yep, in this world writing people are basically the opposite of measurement people. Which side are you on?
reading_mnemonic: Whenever it's you versus someone else, you wear a tie (たい). Naturally, your tie is always the opposite color of your opponent's tie. Kinda like how political rivals wear different color ties when they debate. It's pretty silly, but at least your tie makes it clear that it's you versus them.

meaning_mnemonic: Your nation's flag sits on top of a caped mouth. This is the symbol for the "Bureau of Secret Things." It's a special department of your government made to keep things hidden.
reading_mnemonic: The bureau's best-kept secret is cloaking devices that cloak you (きょく) with the press of a button.

meaning_mnemonic: You see a manhole lid and a towel, both with the name of a city on them. Decorative manhole lids and souvenir towels — two things cities love to slap their names on, especially in Japan.
reading_mnemonic: This city must have a lot of sheep (し) because, besides the manhole lid and the towel, all you can see are sheep. There are sheep everywhere. It's a sheep city.

meaning_mnemonic: In a yurt you use a towel as a seat.
reading_mnemonic: Something about using a towel for a seat is very sexy (せき) to you. Probably because you associate it with sexy people using towel seats on the beach.

meaning_mnemonic: A viking with a mouth towel is a totally normal thing. It's ordinary.
reading_mnemonic: It's normal for a viking to have a mouth towel, but your sloppy farmhand friend Joe(じょう) has a mouth towel too. That's a habit that's only normal for vikings, so why does he have one?

meaning_mnemonic: If you want to dry your horns you need to lay them flat. If they aren't flat they'll always be a little damp somewhere and you'll never have a moment's peace.
reading_mnemonic: Being flat isn't enough, so you cover the whole thing in hay (へい). Hay absorbs water, so you add a flat layer of it.

meaning_mnemonic: Put a lid on something spicy and you'll cook up pure happiness.
reading_mnemonic: Out of spicy foods you made pure happiness. You give it to your sad friend こういち, who waits at the table.

meaning_mnemonic: Under a canopy, there are two persons on the dirt. What do they do there? They sit. The people use the dirt under the canopy as a seat for their butts.
reading_mnemonic: Who decided people have to sit like this? The Czar (ざ). The Czar wants to be above everyone, so he makes them sit on the dirt under canopies while he goes around on horseback or something, towering over them as they sit.

meaning_mnemonic: There's a canopy and a man called the Yoga King standing in the middle of your garden.
reading_mnemonic: Not only is this Yoga King taking over your garden, but he's ordering you to serve food to his class. "You there, peasant, fetch these people your freshest tater (てい) tots from this puny garden to give them strength."

meaning_mnemonic: A good ceremony is under construction for a long time. You can't just make up a new ceremony on the spot. A ceremony is done a certain way because that's the way it's always been done. In short, to build a ceremony, you have to create a ritual first. Then, the ritual can be constructed into a bigger, more lavish ceremony. This kanji also means equation for some reason. Just think of a ceremony that involves doing math and solving equations. How strange would that be? Pretend you're at this ceremony.
reading_mnemonic: So, you're at a ritual, but not just any old ritual. This is a full-blown ceremony and it's incredibly chic (しき). Imagine just how chic it is. Give it a shot — I'll let you come up with the chicness this time (it's good practice).

meaning_mnemonic: If you have a bow and a stick you need to pull the two back together to shoot it. If you can't pull it, you won't be shooting anything.
reading_mnemonic: When you pull the bow back, your body strains and you feel an immense heat (ひ) rise inside of you. You keep pulling and the heat grows hotter and hotter.

meaning_mnemonic: What superhero is most like a triceratops? …If you said Wolverine, you're correct! Why is that the right answer? Because the triceratops has three horns, and Wolverine has three blades coming out of his hands. It's obvious, isn't it? But you knew that of course.
reading_mnemonic: Because you got the answer correct, you win a free trip to とうきょう. Congrats!

meaning_mnemonic: You're walking at night when you discover a lantern covered entirely in hair, making it a very strange shape. In fact, this is a form you'd never expect a lantern to take.
reading_mnemonic: You stare at the shape until you finally recognize it: cake (けい)! Well, it's hairy, glowing cake, but it's still shaped like a big slice of cake.

meaning_mnemonic: You loiter around with a weapon because you're currently doing your service and duty to your country. You're standing guard outside, waiting just in case something will happen.
reading_mnemonic: You're about halfway through your service, when a yak (やく) walks by. It stops directly in front of you and grunts. "Excuse me, Mr. Yak, but it's my duty to escort you away from my country."

meaning_mnemonic: “Don’t loiter – run, Junior!” said Indiana Jones Senior to Indiana Jones Junior. They’re escaping from a sticky situation and Junior was just loitering around like a fool. It’s no time to loiter, it’s time to run!
reading_mnemonic: Deciding not to loiter any longer, Indiana Jones Junior takes his dad’s advice and starts to run. Unfortunately he wasn’t paying attention to where his feet were and he stubbed his toe (と) on a jagged rock. His toe is in so much pain that he can’t bear to run any longer.

meaning_mnemonic: If you loiter around the sun temple, it's likely you'll acquire something. When you loiter around like that it looks like you're waiting for something, so if someone puts something in your hands and you just happen to acquire it, well, no one can fault you for that.
reading_mnemonic: You managed to acquire some tobacco, but just as you're about to leave Tokugawa (とく) Ieyasu comes marching up to you!! Or at least, his ghost does. He stares you dead in the eyes and says, "I didn't found the shogunate for you to acquire illegal goods and kill your body toking on my soil."

meaning_mnemonic: Your heart has a slide running through it because you want to be certain that the blood is flowing in and out of it smoothly. Given how important this is, you want to be absolutely certain.
reading_mnemonic: To be certain that the heart-slide is working, the doctor who put it there hits (ひつ) you in the chest a few times as a test.

meaning_mnemonic: The death of your heart will cause you to forget all of the most important things. People think memories are kept in your brain, but that's not true. Your heart is where all of your most precious memories are kept, and when it dies, you forget them all.
reading_mnemonic: When someone forgets everything they're left with only one thing to do: go bowling (ぼう). Bowling is easy, and there's nothing to forget. You pick up a ball. You drop it. Everything else is automatically taken care of.

meaning_mnemonic: You'll work your soul to death if you're too busy. Being busy just isn't good for your soul. Take breaks. Go on vacation. Don't be so busy that you destroy yourself.
reading_mnemonic: Take time out of your busy life and go bowling (ぼう) once in a while. In fact, you should probably go bowling once a week at least. Nothing brings energy back to your life like some relaxing bowling.

meaning_mnemonic: If you live in the now, there’s a good chance your heart controls your thought process. You don’t have time to think with your brain, you need an answer now so you use your heart to make decisions and thought process.
reading_mnemonic: You're living in the now and letting your heart control all your thoughts. Why are you following your heart? You found you only have one 年 (ねん) to live, so you have to live for the now.

meaning_mnemonic: Everyone has a soul in their life, and that soul shapes their gender. It's not just about body parts — it's about what's inside. In the end, it's one's nature that truly matters.
reading_mnemonic: Once you've decided what your gender is, someone comes to your house and lays a saber (せい) on your shoulders. "This is now your nature," they say, lifting the saber. It's official! It's in all the newspapers, there's a parade, and everyone pats you on the back. Thanks, gender saber!

meaning_mnemonic: Imagining one’s self without a heart can make it hard to draw breath. Without a heart, you’d have no blood pumping and you would start to die. This would make it increasingly harder to draw breath and get oxygen to stay alive.
reading_mnemonic: You know how when people are unconscious and their breath slows or comes to a stop, they use smelling salts to revive them? Well a smelly sock (そく) can work just as well. Socks get really stinky and their stench is powerful enough to revive someone who isn’t drawing breath.

meaning_mnemonic: A criminal's heart will always be sad. No one chooses a life of crime if they're happy. And even if they seem like they're doing fine on the outside, deep down they're really sad.
reading_mnemonic: The sad feelings fill the criminal's body with heat (ひ). This heat spreads and radiates out. If you walk next to them on the street, you'll feel the sad heat floating by you.

meaning_mnemonic: Your soul is blue. As in, it's sad and not feeling well. This is because your soul changes colors depending on your feelings or what emotions you're expressing.
reading_mnemonic: Why is your soul feeling blue? Because Joe (じょう), the big local farmhand, was extremely mean to you.

meaning_mnemonic: Only a tree with eyes and a heart has the ability to imagine and to contemplate. For a tree to imagine and contemplate things, it needs eyes to see and a heart to feel.
reading_mnemonic: If a tree can imagine, it likely has a soul (そう). Its soul is what makes it possible for the tree to contemplate things, you see?

meaning_mnemonic: Put on cleats so you can plant a kiss on your sweetheart's forehead in the heart of winter — that's love. You'll be braving the harsh winter elements for love, so you put on your cleats to get a better grip on the snow. Sure, you could just wait for better weather to go see them, but then it wouldn't be true love, would it?
reading_mnemonic: Walking through the winter snow with your cleats on, you've gotta keep your eye (あい) on the prize. It's a really hard journey, but you keep your eye on the prize, which is your love and the time you'll get to spend with them.

meaning_mnemonic: When a canine puts its mouth on your heart, it's a pretty unforgettable feeling.
reading_mnemonic: Overall, though, it's a good feeling — so good that you feel like Genghis Khan (かん)! With this canine lovingly slobbering on your heart, you feel like you could go out and conquer the world!

meaning_mnemonic: When a drunkard holds a sword it becomes something else. The drunkard doesn't become a swordsman, they're still just a drunkard. But the sword in their hands does.
reading_mnemonic: The sword has become a saber (せい)! It's just like the saber you have! Hey, wait.

meaning_mnemonic: A simple drunkard starting a war.
reading_mnemonic: The simple drunkard started a war with the centaurs (せん)! This is especially unfortunate, because the centaurs are really good at battles because they're all automatically cavalry troops.

meaning_mnemonic: You're tearing this door down with an axe. You're absolutely crazy. "I HATE THIS PLACE!!" you keep yelling as you smash in the door.
reading_mnemonic: You smash through the door and finally get inside the place, only to find some kind of show (しょ) going on. It's a circus show — elephants, tightrope walkers, bears on unicycles! The greatest show on earth, but why is it at this place?

meaning_mnemonic: On the ground you put barbs at the bottom of a slide. This is your special talent. When you go down the slide, you fly right past the barbs like some kind of daredevil. Any normal kid would land on the barbs and get hurt, but you have this talent.
reading_mnemonic: But then people start to say that no human could have so much talent, that you must be a cyborg (さい). Are you really a talented cyborg?

meaning_mnemonic: Take your fingers to the street to hit some people! Street fingers are for curling into a fist. And that street fist wants to do some hitting!
reading_mnemonic: As you hit one chump after another, suddenly your dad (だ) comes marching out of your house. Uh oh. Dad caught you hitting, which, honestly, isn't a very nice thing to do, so he has every right to stop you.

meaning_mnemonic: In your fingers is a weapon, so you throw it. Maybe you're angry and you threw the weapon at a person you don't like. Maybe you're a pacifist and you threw it away so no one else could use it. Either way, when you have a weapon in your fingers you have to throw it.
reading_mnemonic: You throw your weapon away because you're about to enter とうきょう and there are no weapons allowed there. There is, however, a big pile of thrown away weapons by the border, which is where you're throwing yours right now.

meaning_mnemonic: If your fingers are strong enough, you can take an axe and fold it in half. But be careful not to bend it too far, or you might just break it!
reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, as you fold these axes in half you realize they come in sets (せつ), so there are twice the axes you thought there would be. To compensate, you start folding them in sets too.

meaning_mnemonic: Try to use your fingers to spoon out some of the sun and you'll come back with just one finger.
reading_mnemonic: Don't worry, you aren't the only one out there with just one finger, sheep (し) only have one finger too. I mean, they're hooves, which are really just a single animal finger. It's just big and kind of flat.

meaning_mnemonic: The branch radical and the branch kanji are the same! This kanji also means support. To remember it, think about a tree with lots of branches. The branches support each other and the trunk of the tree. If you were to climb the tree, the branches would be able to support your weight too!
reading_mnemonic: You're happily sitting on this branch, letting it support all this weight, when a sheep (し) starts to climb the tree. A very, very big sheep. Uh oh... no no, sheep. If you get on this branch it won't be able to support all this weight!!!

meaning_mnemonic: As the year starts moving in the direction of winter, the trees must release their leaves.
reading_mnemonic: The trees release all of their leaves onto your home (ほう). Slowly, you watch in horror as your home is consumed by the released leaves. They enter in through the windows, doors, and the chimney.

meaning_mnemonic: It's correct in winter to focus on politics and the government. Elections are happening, in the new year politicians are being sworn in. Winter is government time!
reading_mnemonic: Everyone involved in politics and government wields a special saber (せい). If two political parties are arguing, they'll whip out their sabers and start slashing away!

meaning_mnemonic: A shellfish that can't live through winter is a failure. Any proper shellfish would survive through the winter, so this is quite an embarrassing defeat.
reading_mnemonic: The best way to avoid failure is to say a little haiku (はい) to distract you from the cold. In fact, this can work in any situation where you're afraid of defeat. Say a haiku aloud, it will calm your nerves and warm you from the inside.

meaning_mnemonic: Give rice to a woman in winter so she can count it. The woman will count each individual grain of rice, then tell you the amount or number of grains.
reading_mnemonic: Why do you have to count your rice out like this? It's because someone sued (すう) your farm and took everything you owned. Since being sued, you only have a small amount of rice to last the winter.

meaning_mnemonic: The easy radical and the easy kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: What would be an easy reading for this kanji? い! The sound easy starts with!

meaning_mnemonic: You've been playing blackjack in the sun since long ago. This is the longest game of blackjack you've ever played and it feels like ages since you started. You've been sitting out in the sun playing blackjack since long, long ago.
reading_mnemonic: Once you finally finish the game, you walk the long walk back home, in the sun, barefoot, on a dirt road that hasn't been maintained since long ago. Your feet are all sweaty from being out in the sun, and walking on this dirt road gives you muck ashi (むかし). Your ashi (feet) are all mucky and muddy from the combination of dirt and sweat. Your muck ashi are really gross, man.

meaning_mnemonic: Once the sun comes out, you can use this key to unlock it and take you to any previous day, even just yesterday! The sun is in charge of the day changes, so if you use a key to unlock it, you can control the flow of time and return to yesterday, or a previous day in the past. Behold the power of the sun.
reading_mnemonic: Time traveling to a previous time, like yesterday, can be rough on the body. As such, you wear a small sack (さく) to hold your valuables while you're ripped through the sands of time. The sack keeps your important stuff from getting lost. The sack holds your key to the sun as well.

meaning_mnemonic: The sun has an excuse for disappearing at night. The sun gets really tired, same as anyone else – so when night rolls around the sun excuses itself and goes to sleep. It’s a valid excuse.
reading_mnemonic: Unfortunately, you also have a history of overworking yourself, so you've been outright banned (ばん) from showing up at night.

meaning_mnemonic: The sun is out, the sky is blue, things have begun to clear up!
reading_mnemonic: Now that it's starting to clear up you can't help but laugh. "Ha (は)! Ha ha ha!" you laugh up into the sky. The sun feels great on your face, making you feel lively! And that blue sky ain't too shabby either.

meaning_mnemonic: If the sun starts to make a sound, you know it's about to go dark. The sun isn't supposed to make a sound, so if you can hear it, it's probably about to fizzle out or something. After it's gone, obviously everything will be pitch black. Get ready to be in the dark!
reading_mnemonic: Now wandering around your house in the dark you start to feel hungry, so you reach blindly for some food and take a bite. Yuck! It's anchovies (あん). You don't even like anchovies, how did they get in your house? Hmm… Dark forces are at work here…

meaning_mnemonic: There are mouths, twenty of them, singing beautiful music together. The music seems to bend toward you through the air.
reading_mnemonic: The twenty mouths make so much music that they literally cloak you (きょく) with it. They cloak you with the music.

meaning_mnemonic: Let the sun shine into your ear while sitting on a stool and make sure most of it gets in your head. You want to fill your brain with the most sun anyone ever has.
reading_mnemonic: Most of this is for your cyborg (さい). You're testing out a new way to power it, but if you can't get most of the sun into your ear, it won't be enough to power most of the cyborg's robo-parts.

meaning_mnemonic: Causing death at every turn, the moon king sits inside his moon, getting ready to cause death on anything in his sights. Sounds a lot like the Death Star from a certain movie. One of which is "Star Wars: A New Hope."
reading_mnemonic: The name A New Hope, as we all know, comes from the ending where the moon king's son sends a bowling (ぼう) ball into that little opening and knocks it out of the sky.

meaning_mnemonic: A "crab moon" is a specific period of time.
reading_mnemonic: When the crab moon period of time is upon us, we must take a special key (き) and lock everything in such a way that crabs cannot get in.

meaning_mnemonic: You're flying in a jet. Even though it's one of the fastest things on earth, your child is sitting in the back asking, "Are we there yet? Are we there yet?" You have to keep responding. "Not yet! Not yet! NOT YET!"
reading_mnemonic: What a selfish kid, right? Well, all he thinks about is "Me (み) me me me me me me me me me me." Hate kids like that.

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji uses a modified jet radical. The front area of the wing is wider than the middle area of the wing. This may seem counterintuitive, but by doing this they can fit so much more jet fuel. The jet zooms off and keeps going for a long, long time, until it reaches the end of the earth.
reading_mnemonic: When you get to the end of the world, you land your jet and put out a few mats (まつ) to sit on so you can view the sights.

meaning_mnemonic: The bundle radical and the bundle kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: You should always bundle your socks (そく). If you don't, there is a 100% chance you'll lose all of the left ones.

meaning_mnemonic: The fruit radical and the fruit kanji are exactly the same! Bodacious!
reading_mnemonic: They sell fruit at the store, and you need to drive your car (か) to get there. A car is the fastest way to fruit.

meaning_mnemonic: If a tree wants to kiss you, it's a sign of your status. Only someone of high status would be worthy enough to receive the gnarly but gentle kiss of a tree. Trees don't kiss just anyone, you know.
reading_mnemonic: The best way to convince a tree of your status is to say "cock-a-doodle-doo" at it, like a cock (かく), i.e. a male chicken. Trees really place a lot of status on the ability to sound like a cock crowing.

meaning_mnemonic: By a tree, there's a sheep in the water with a formal name ender. That means everyone calls him Sheep-sama. No one calls him just "Sheep," since he's kind of a big deal. He's actually like sheep royalty. When he's not in his castle, Sheep-sama enjoys playing in the water by the trees. This can also mean manner, as in your manner of doing things. I guess someone with a formal name ender has a different manner of doing things.
reading_mnemonic: This sheep with the formal name ender only likes to play outside in the water during the summer (さま). Summer is the best season for this fancy sheep. The other seasons just can't compare.

meaning_mnemonic: Under a tree, a broken arrow protrudes from a turkey. It was fighting for the rights of its fellow turkeys, and was mortally wounded in the process.
reading_mnemonic: "You have rights, so I won't shoot you like this turkey," says the voice of Ken (けん) the samurai, from above you in the tree.

meaning_mnemonic: The tree marked with a yellow X on the side of the house is going to get cut down. You’ve marked it with a yellow X so the hired help knows which tree to cut down. There are a lot of trees on the side of the house, but the tree marked with a yellow X is the only one in danger of causing damage to your roof in the event of a storm.
reading_mnemonic: Wait, that woman with the chainsaw is Yoko (よこ) Ono! Yes, the same Yoko Ono who’s married to John Lennon of the Beatles. What’s she doing chopping down trees on the side of your house? Who can say. Silly Yoko.

meaning_mnemonic: Next to a tree, you spot poop, not once but twice. Only a drunkard would be the type of person to not use the nearby machine toilet. There's a perfectly good outhouse with a machine toilet right there, but this drunkard is so drunk that he decides to poop under the tree instead. And not only does he poop once, he poops twice.
reading_mnemonic: Oh, I see — the door to the outhouse with the machine toilet is locked, and the drunkard doesn't have the key (き). If he had a machine like a jackhammer, or a circular saw, or some other heavy duty machine, he might be able to get in without a key, but since he has none of those or a key, he's reduced to pooping under the tree instead.
radical_breakdown: 木|Tree, 幺|Poop, 戈|Drunkard, 人|Person

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical it comes from. Lack becomes Lack!
reading_mnemonic: To remember けつ, we use the word "ketsup." It's the perfect blend of ketchup and catsup! You're lacking something in your fridge. You look around, trying to find the ketsup (けつ) you lack. You can't find it, because you lack it.

meaning_mnemonic: Ice is what you're lacking, so the next thing you need to do is go to the store and see if they have any. Nope, no ice. So, now you go to the next store. Is there ice here? Nope. Next!
reading_mnemonic: To remember the reading じ, we used the word "Jesus" - Finally, when you're at the last store in existence, you decide it's time to pray to Jesus (じ), asking for a miracle. He comes down from the heavens with ice in his hands.

meaning_mnemonic: Stop! That box of rice is actually full of teeth! I know it says "rice" on the cover, but I promise you those are all teeth and if you bite into them you'll break a tooth of your own.
reading_mnemonic: Why do I have a rice box full of teeth? Ha (は)! Wouldn't you like to know. Ha! I definitely have an answer that isn't weird or creepy. Ha... ha ha...

meaning_mnemonic: Yakuza bars barely exist. The remainder of them aren't even in Japan.
reading_mnemonic: The remainder of the yakuza bars aren't in Japan. Strangely, they are all in Zanzibar (ざん).

meaning_mnemonic: There's treasure in this tree so you take out your weapon and kill it.
reading_mnemonic: But after the kill, Satsuki (さつ) appears and yells at you. She likes trees — remember how she protected one in the 札 mnemonic? — so Satsuki's pretty upset you'd kill one like that.

meaning_mnemonic: The mouth clan are a group of people. They are the people of a nation.
reading_mnemonic: The mouth clan peoples are a nation of people who use their mouths to say mean (みん) things to other peoples.

meaning_mnemonic: Look at the ground! You spilled some water drops, so I request that you wipe them up. I'd do it myself, but you're the one who spilled them, so I'm requesting that you do it. Pretty reasonable request, right?
reading_mnemonic: Oh, one more thing. I request that you wipe up the water with this cucumber (きゅう).

meaning_mnemonic: You have at your disposal a tsunami to assassinate this person, or a hook. Which method will you choose? Decide now!
reading_mnemonic: To remember the けつ reading, we always use the word "ketsup." It's a special mix of ketchup and catsup (yum): You finally decide. You're going to go with the tsunami... but not just any tsunami. You'll kill him with a tsunami of ketsup (けつ).

meaning_mnemonic: After a tsunami, use this machine to cure the people and the country from the damage. Healing machines are all over Japan just in case a tsunami does way more damage than they can handle. Oh, and whoever cures and heals the most people will be able to rule over them once everything starts going back to normal. So keep that in mind, kay?
reading_mnemonic: Alternative ways to cure yourself after a tsunami are either praying to Jesus (じ) or eating your weight in cheese (ち). I'm not sure if I have enough cheese for all the people that got hit though... Hmm, do you have cheese? Before you make your decision, remember that whoever cures you will be able to reign over you and your people. So do you want to be led by Jesus or by some cheese? The choice is yours.

meaning_mnemonic: Tsunamis in the past changed the methods and laws of today.
reading_mnemonic: These methods and laws affected your own home (ほう) the most.

meaning_mnemonic: If a tsunami is going to last an eternity you better learn how to swim now. We'll be under water for the rest of time and if you can't swim you're not gonna make it.
reading_mnemonic: Oy (およ)! Oy, stop daydreaming about swimming and actually do it!

meaning_mnemonic: A tsunami previously gave everything in this town a good wash. There are many laundromats in this town, so when the previous tsunami hit, all of the detergent mixed with the water and gave everything a good wash.
reading_mnemonic: It wasn't just the town that got a wash, it was the centaurs (せん) too. (Centaurs happen to live in this town.) And being half horse, centaurs have a lot of hair that needs washing. Luckily, the soap tsunami gave them a good wash too.

meaning_mnemonic: A tsunami of tongues is coming at you. As it washes over you, you feel each individual tongue moving around on your body, licking you. They make you feel so... lively!
reading_mnemonic: This lively feeling isn't just happening to you, the tongue tsunami is licking it into all of the cats (かつ) in your neighborhood too!

meaning_mnemonic: A tsunami lifts all the trash out of the river and it streams out onto the shores.
reading_mnemonic: Next to the trash stream you suddenly see Ryu (りゅう) from Street Fighter and he looks pissed. He's furious that so many people throw their trash in the river and it causes streams like this.

meaning_mnemonic: A long time ago a huge tsunami swept a triceratops up into the moon and extinguished its life.
reading_mnemonic: This famous event where almost all life was extinguished is reenacted every year for the Shougun (しょう). He's got a bit of an unhealthy obsession with extinguishing life...

meaning_mnemonic: You see a tsunami that's simultaneous (with another tsunami, I assume) and you know the world is about to come to an end.
reading_mnemonic: Just as the world is about to come to an end, your cyborg (さい) appears and blocks it with its cyborg body!

meaning_mnemonic: There's a tsunami coming and you want to be together with it by yourself (oneself) so you go to the harbor.
reading_mnemonic: As you look around at the harbor in your last moments you suddenly see someone in the water. It's こういち! He's sitting in an inner tube in the harbor waiting for the tsunami too.

meaning_mnemonic: Your fortune boils down to a single point in time. One point in time determines how the rest of your future will go.
reading_mnemonic: As you stare at the point, you watch in awe as it moves to the ten (てん) spot in a long series of numbers.

meaning_mnemonic: Under a misshapen crescent moon, a dog boils as much nature as it can find.
reading_mnemonic: Destroying nature like this is the dog's way of practicing Zen (ぜん) Buddhism. As it breathes in the fumes from all of the different pieces of nature being boiled down, the dog gets really zen and chill.

meaning_mnemonic: If you have a fire and a helicopter hovering beside it, there's going to be a lot of dirt and smoke billowing around. Mostly smoke, on account of the fire. Now it's in your eyes and mouth. It gets in your lungs and you can't breathe. Why, helicopter, why!
reading_mnemonic: The smoke is too much and you realize this is the end (えん) for you. You're gonna die here!

meaning_mnemonic: Your womb spins in a circle and starts to boil with heat. Uh oh, I think you have a fever.
reading_mnemonic: The heat from your fever is making your insides and your head and your entire body spin and boil, until your doctor throws some nets (ねつ) around you. You were flailing around and they couldn't get you to stop, so they had to catch you in a series of nets.

meaning_mnemonic: In the animal kingdom, a snake is the most likely to commit a crime. Remember the Garden of Eden? The snake was the bad guy. Ever since then, snakes are the animal most known for committing crimes.
reading_mnemonic: This snake has evaded the law for too long. It’s time for a true hero to put an end to its crime spree. Enter Han (はん) Solo. Han Solo is the only man strong and brave enough to put an end to this snake and his crime filled ways.

meaning_mnemonic: If you see an animal among the flowers in a rice paddy, chances are it’s a cat. Cats love rice paddy flowers, almost as much as they love catnip.
reading_mnemonic: Wait a minute… This cat is pretty odd looking. You take a closer look, seeing it is missing its neck (ねこ). You go to pet it, but it's super sensitive about that area of its head, which is basically a face connected to a body...

meaning_mnemonic: The king radical and the king kanji are the same!
reading_mnemonic: When you see the king you need to say, "Oh (おう) King! Oh King, oh no, oh why are you looking at me like that? Oh King... you aren't going to chop off my head are you? OH NO!"

meaning_mnemonic: The king requests a sphere!
reading_mnemonic: The sphere is a cucumber (きゅう) sphere. A strange sphere shaped cucumber.

meaning_mnemonic: You stand on the Cliff of Life and give birth to a child. Oh no! You’re standing too close to the edge of the Cliff of Life! The baby falls off the cliff right after you give birth to it! In your despair, you throw all your property off the cliff too.
reading_mnemonic: You give birth, and now this happens. Such bad luck. But wait! What's that sound? Sleigh bells? Could it be?! It's Santa-san (さん)! He caught your baby! And all your property.

meaning_mnemonic: A giant cross with a mouth stands above you. "I am reason!" it says to you. It is the Cross of Reason.
reading_mnemonic: The reason that this Cross of Reason exists is to combat the youths (ゆう) of the world, who just bring chaos into everything.

meaning_mnemonic: There's a cross inside your mouth, so the things you say are very pious. Everything you say, you say humbly.
reading_mnemonic: As you're saying all these humble things, you're also mowing (もう) your neighbor's lawn. Your neighbors love you so much, because you're so humble, and you mow their lawn for them.

meaning_mnemonic: A group of private sword guys are in your rice paddy. You must detain them at once! Private sword guys are people who work for private companies and use their swords on people. They're basically paid assassins. And you're going to detain them!
reading_mnemonic: You're running out of steam and you're afraid you might not be able to detain all of these guys when Ryu (りゅう) from Street Fighter appears. He hates swords, and will only use fists because it's the honorable way to fight, so he starts helping you detain them! He's also found a loophole (る) in the system and you don't have to be super gentle with these guys either. So detain them as forcefully as you want. It is your rice paddy they're in, after all.

meaning_mnemonic: You have to sickle the rice paddy today because it's your turn. This kanji also means number in a series, which is a lot like a turn. For example, you're number 3, so your turn will be number 3.
reading_mnemonic: This turn-based rice sickle system is a contest as well! But, you are disappointed to find out that you have been banned (ばん) from the game because of the performance enhancing steroids you've been taking.

meaning_mnemonic: You reach for a spoon to start eating, but your mama hands you an arrow instead and points towards the coat rack. Hm, that's not like her… Suddenly you're filled with doubt. Is this really your mama? You doubt it.
reading_mnemonic: Now full of doubt, you decide to test your mama by putting her in a guillotine (ぎ). It sounds harsh, but the guillotine is the only way to clear up your doubts.
radical_breakdown: 匕|Spoon, マ|Mama, 矢|Arrow, 疋|Coat Rack

meaning_mnemonic: There's a tent of beans. You try to climb it.
reading_mnemonic: You climb the bean tent, and from this vantage point you can see とうきょう in the distance.

meaning_mnemonic: If you compare white light to the other colors you'll realize... white consists of all the colors in one. It contains all the colors in the spectrum in one color. It is the one color that is everything.
reading_mnemonic: You decide white light is the ultimate color. You decide you want to put it on all things to make everything white. "What a great idea," you think. You try to put it on everything and you nearly succeed... except, the miners (みな). They keep getting dirty doing all their mining things. NOOO, your plan is ruined!

meaning_mnemonic: This kanji is the same as the radical — straight as straight can be. It can also mean direct, because when you go straight to a place, you're going there directly. Depending on the context it can even mean fix, since fixing something means straightening out all the messed up crooked bits.
reading_mnemonic: Put food straight into your esophagus without chewing and you will choke (ちょく). You want to get straight to the most important part of eating — the digesting part — but if you don't follow all the intermediate steps, you'll end up choking.

meaning_mnemonic: You need to look a tree in the eye to gain a mutual respect for each other. Stand up straight, look the tree directly in its eye(s). If it looks right back, you know things are mutual.
reading_mnemonic: If your respect for the tree is mutual with the respect the tree feels for you, you'll be able to see the tree's soul (そう). Right now its soul looks pretty sad, like it's trying to say, "Why are your people cutting down all my friends? I thought we had a mutual understanding."

meaning_mnemonic: The stone radical and stone kanji are the same thing!
reading_mnemonic: You throw a stone through a window... and, now you can see something very sexy (せき).

meaning_mnemonic: You take a stone to the forehead of a turkey. It is certain that you will damage it.
reading_mnemonic: You're killing this turkey, and you need to make sure he's dead for certain. The reason you need to make sure this turkey is dead is because of the cock (かく) in your life. Male chickens get really jealous when turkeys are around.

meaning_mnemonic: What do you get if you lend a spirit your umbrella? Thanks, of course! Especially if that spirit is Totoro, the spirit of the forest.
reading_mnemonic: So what did you receive as a thanks? You open it up, and there's a ray (れい) gun inside!

meaning_mnemonic: Your spirit should feel humble before a god's spirit. You never really feel humble in front of anyone else, but if you meet a god's spirit… Well, you should probably lower yourself appropriately. Gods have powerful spirits.
reading_mnemonic: When you meet a god's spirit, you need to get down on your shins (しん). Get down on your ankles? No, not low enough. Knees? No, no, get your shins flat on the ground to show how humble you really are. Luckily, you're wearing jeans (じん), so at least that will stop your poor shins getting chafed!

meaning_mnemonic: When a spirit decides to live in your scarecrow, you'll be granted good luck and good fortune. Crows won't hang out in your farm. Everything you grow will become large and delicious. But not everyone is so lucky that a spirit will decide to live in their scarecrow. So maybe the luck was in you all along!
reading_mnemonic: You want to check the scarecrow to make sure your recent luck is coming from it, so you kick it. "F*** (ふく) you!" it yells. Oh yeah, there's a spirit in there.

meaning_mnemonic: You scoop some grains into a ladle to do science. You're doing experiments on these grains in your science course.
reading_mnemonic: Using your science skills, the right temperatures and measurements, you manage to get these grains to grow into a car (か). This is the science department's special car now!

meaning_mnemonic: If a grain seems extra heavy, you know it's a different kind. Not all types of grains are the same. So when you feel the heavy type, you know it isn't the same as the light kind.
reading_mnemonic: You sort all of the different kinds and types by putting them in the right chutes (しゅ). They slide away, probably to some big type-based piles you can't see.

meaning_mnemonic: Bamboo heaven is a place for laughing. Bamboo is a very jolly plant, and they love to laugh. Even after death in bamboo heaven, the bamboo continue to laugh joyfully. Bamboo heaven is truly a place of laughter.
reading_mnemonic: There’s actually a war a goin’ on up in that there bamboo heaven, y’know? Ye might not have heard of it with all that there laughin’ a goin’ on, but there definitely be a war a (わら) goin’ on up in bamboo heaven, y’hear? The bamboo are scared so that’s why they be laughin’ so much. They nervous.

meaning_mnemonic: The bamboo temple is equal to all of the other non-bamboo temples. Just because it's made of bamboo doesn't make it any less special and spiritual.
reading_mnemonic: The bamboo temple is also an equal distance away from the other temples in とうきょう. When you look at a map of とうきょう temples, you can measure them out and they'll all be perfectly equal.

meaning_mnemonic: With the bamboo from that tree, your trained eye can tell it'll make an excellent box. Boxes made from bamboo trees are very sturdy and fashionable. You have an eye for fashion as well, you see.
